transitionIn.text: 167 BC. The Second Temple has stood for generations in a small province. New empires have come, and a crisis is about to break over the way of life of this people. To see how it began, the chapter goes back to Alexander.

vignette.caption: The Second Temple in Yehud (impression)

steps.text: Our last chapter ended in the Persian period. Some of Judah's people had come home, and a Second Temple stood in a small province called Yehud.
Now it is one hundred and sixty seven BC. A Greek-speaking king, ruling from Syria, stands over this land, and the Temple is about to enter a crisis.
claims: In 167 BC a Seleucid king rules this land, and Jewish books remember a crisis over the Temple.
steps.display: Now it is 167 BC. A Greek-speaking king, ruling from Syria, stands over this land, and the Temple is about to enter a crisis.

vignette.alt: Jerusalem on a ridge at dusk, a temple platform above tight streets, a tense stillness in the air
vignette.caption: A crisis is coming (impression)

steps.text: The Second Temple still stands. But the empire that first let the exiles return has passed away, and new kingdoms have taken its place.
claims: After Persia, Hellenistic kingdoms rule the land around the Second Temple.

steps.text: How did a revolt begin in these hills? And how was the Temple dedicated again? To find out, we go back.

On the map, Yehud is still a small province around Jerusalem. To the west lies the sea, with Greek-speaking cities on the coast. Far to the north is Antioch, a new royal capital in Syria. To the south-west, Alexandria in Egypt.
claims: Yehud is a small province around Jerusalem, with Hellenistic royal cities to the north and south-west.

steps.text: In the books later called Maccabees, and in Josephus, this is the hour when Jewish law is forbidden, and an alien altar is set on the Temple mount. How far that was royal policy, and how far a fight inside Jerusalem, scholars still dispute.
claims: The books of the Maccabees and Josephus describe a ban on the law and an alien altar in 167 BC.
How far this was royal policy, and how far a conflict inside Jerusalem, is disputed.

steps.text: That is the world of this chapter. Now the story begins.

transitionOut.text: Next: a Roman general in Jerusalem, and the end of Hasmonean independence.

events.title: Alexander and the new world
events.text: In 332 BC Alexander of Macedon takes the Persian empire. The Greek historian Arrian records his long sieges of Tyre and of Gaza, on the road to Egypt. The story that he visited Jerusalem and honoured the Temple is told by Josephus, writing centuries later; it is not in the Greek historians of Alexander. When Alexander dies in 323 BC, his generals divide the lands.
events.why: The sieges of Tyre and Gaza are in a Greek historian of Alexander. The visit to Jerusalem is a later Jewish tradition.
claims: In 332 BC Alexander takes Tyre and Gaza on his way to Egypt.
Josephus says Alexander visited Jerusalem and honoured the Temple.
The Greek historians of Alexander do not tell that visit.

events.title: From Ptolemy to Seleucus
events.text: Judaea first lies under the Ptolemies, who rule from Alexandria in Egypt. In about 200 BC, after a battle at Paneas under Mount Hermon, recorded by Polybius, the land passes to the Seleucid kings, who rule from Antioch in Syria. For a time, Jewish life in Jerusalem goes on: a high priest, the Second Temple, a small people under a distant king.
events.why: The change of empire is in a Greek historian who knew this world. The daily life of the province is reconstructed from later Jewish books and from the pattern of Hellenistic rule.
claims: In the third century BC Judaea lies under the Ptolemies, ruling from Alexandria.
After the battle of Paneas, c. 200 BC, the land passes from the Ptolemies to the Seleucids.

events.title: Jason, Menelaus, and a Greek Jerusalem
events.text: The second book of the Maccabees says that in 175 BC a man called Jason, of the priestly house, obtains the high priesthood from Antiochus and seeks to make Jerusalem more like a Greek city, with a gymnasium. He is later displaced, in that account, by Menelaus, who is not of the old high-priestly line. How far this was a culture war, and how far a fight among priestly families for power and tax, scholars do not agree.
events.why: A struggle over the high priesthood in these years is widely accepted. The details, and what they meant, follow later Jewish books and are read in more than one way.
claims: 2 Maccabees says Jason obtains the high priesthood in 175 BC and promotes Greek ways in Jerusalem.
2 Maccabees says Menelaus, not of the old high-priestly line, displaces Jason.
Scholars disagree on whether the conflict was mainly cultural, or a struggle among priestly families for power and revenue.

events.title: The Heliodorus stele
events.text: A royal letter on stone, first published in 2007 and with further fragments later found at Maresha in the southern lowlands, shows Seleucid officials already watching over temples and revenues in this region, in the years before the revolt. It does not mention a persecution. Antiochus IV, called Epiphanes, is a real king: his coins, and the historian Polybius, show him campaigning in Egypt.
events.why: The stele is independent evidence of royal oversight of sacred funds. It is not evidence of the later crisis itself.
claims: The Heliodorus stele shows Seleucid oversight of temples and revenues in the region, in the years before the revolt.
Antiochus IV is attested on coins and in Polybius, including campaigns in Egypt.

events.title: The crisis of 167
events.text: In 167 BC, in the usual reckoning, the books of the Maccabees say a persecution begins in Judaea: the law is forbidden, and an alien altar is set upon the altar of the Lord. The book of Daniel and Josephus tell related stories. No royal edict of persecution has been found on stone. Some scholars read a royal attack on Jewish law; others read a civil conflict in Jerusalem, later told as a persecution from outside.
events.why: Several Jewish books close to the time remember a crisis. The inner motives of the king, and the exact acts, are harder to fix, and modern historians do not agree on the balance between royal policy and conflict inside the city.
claims: 1 and 2 Maccabees date a persecution in Judaea to 167 BC, in the usual reckoning.
2 Maccabees and Daniel describe a desolating sacrilege and an alien altar on the Temple altar.
No royal edict of persecution from 167 BC has been found on stone.
Whether 167 BC was mainly a royal persecution or a civil conflict later told as one is disputed.

events.title: The revolt in the hills
events.text: The first book of the Maccabees says the revolt begins at Modein, when a priest called Mattathias refuses a royal command and flees to the hills with his sons. His son Judah, later called Maccabee, becomes the military leader in that tradition. The book tells of fights at Beth-horon and Emmaus. The identification of Modein is not certain, and the troop numbers are often thought to be inflated. A hill war in this landscape is real enough.
events.why: The early battles are told only in later Jewish books. The landscape of a hill war is clear; the heroic numbers and some of the places are not.
claims: 1 Maccabees says the revolt begins at Modein, when Mattathias refuses a royal command.
The site of Modein is disputed.
Troop numbers and the heroic shape of the early battles in 1 Maccabees are disputed; a hill war in this landscape is plausible.

events.title: The Temple rededicated
events.text: In 164 BC, in the usual reckoning, the first book says Jerusalem is retaken, the altar is rebuilt, and the Temple is dedicated again, for eight days. That memory will become the festival of Dedication, later called Hanukkah. The later festival is real; the exact calendar of the first dedication is a traditional reckoning. No certain stone of that restoration has been identified on the mount.
events.why: The dedication is told in 1 Maccabees and remembered in a living festival. Archaeology has not identified the first restored altar.
claims: 1 Maccabees dates a rededication of the Temple, for eight days, to 164 BC in the usual reckoning.
The festival of Dedication (Hanukkah) remembers this story; the exact calendar of the first dedication is a traditional reckoning.
No certain remains of the 164 BC restoration have been identified on the Temple mount.

events.title: A Hasmonean house
events.text: Judah falls in battle, in this tradition, and his brothers Jonathan and Simon take up the lead. In time they are recognised as high priest, and a family from the western hills becomes the ruling house, later called Hasmonean. The first book claims that in Simon's days the yoke of the nations is lifted, and that this house takes the port of Joppa. Later coins will mark the house; the first coins that name it come after these opening years. A reported treaty with Rome is not confirmed by a Roman record of the same years.
events.why: That a Hasmonean house came to rule is not in serious doubt. The first book's claim of independence, the early coins, and the Roman treaty are each read with care.
claims: 1 Maccabees and Josephus say Jonathan, then Simon, are recognised as high priest, and that their house later called Hasmonean rules.
1 Maccabees claims that in Simon's days, usually 142 BC, the yoke of the nations is lifted.
Hasmonean coins appear after the opening years of the revolt, not at its very beginning.
1 Maccabees describes a treaty with Rome; it is not confirmed by a Roman record of those years, and its form is disputed.

claims: 1 and 2 Maccabees date a persecution in Judaea to 167 BC, in the usual reckoning.
steps.display: In 167 BC, or in the Seleucid year usually reckoned so, the books of the Maccabees say a persecution begins in Judaea.

vignette.alt: A tense street below a temple platform, shut doors, empty courts, smoke in the distance
vignette.caption: The crisis remembered (impression)

steps.text: What we can hold to is more modest. A crisis in these years was remembered, close to the time, in several Jewish books. The inner motives of the king, and the exact acts, are harder to fix.
claims: A crisis in these years is remembered in several nearly contemporary Jewish books; the king's motives and the exact acts are harder to fix.

vignette.alt: Quiet limestone hills and a small city on a ridge, open and undecided, morning light
vignette.caption: What the stones can show is limited (impression)

steps.text: The first book of the Maccabees says the revolt begins at Modein, a town in the western hills, when a priest called Mattathias refuses a royal command and flees to the hills with his sons.
claims: 1 Maccabees says the revolt begins at Modein, when Mattathias refuses a royal command.

vignette.alt: A small hill town of stone houses among olive terraces, paths leading into rougher hills
vignette.caption: Modein, in the tradition (impression)

steps.text: In one hundred and sixty four BC, in the usual reckoning, the first book says the altar is rebuilt and the Temple dedicated again, for eight days.
claims: 1 Maccabees dates a rededication of the Temple, for eight days, to 164 BC in the usual reckoning.
steps.display: In 164 BC, in the usual reckoning, the first book says the altar is rebuilt and the Temple dedicated again, for 8 days.

vignette.alt: A newly built stone altar in a modest temple court, simple offerings, people at a distance, no readable writing
vignette.caption: The Temple dedicated again (impression)

steps.text: That memory will become the festival of Dedication, later called Hanukkah. The later festival is real. The exact calendar of the first dedication is a traditional reckoning.
claims: The festival of Dedication (Hanukkah) remembers this story; the exact calendar of the first dedication is a traditional reckoning.

vignette.alt: Small oil lamps glowing in a quiet stone court at night, a modest temple facade, warm lamp light
vignette.caption: The festival of Dedication (impression)

steps.text: In time, Jonathan is recognised as high priest, and Simon after him. A family from the western hills becomes the ruling house, later called Hasmonean.
claims: 1 Maccabees and Josephus say Jonathan, then Simon, are recognised as high priest, and that their house later called Hasmonean rules.

vignette.alt: A small hill state around Jerusalem, terraced slopes, a modest palace-like building and a temple on the ridge
vignette.caption: A ruling house in the hills (impression)

steps.text: The first book also says this house takes the port of Joppa, and so gains a door to the sea.
claims: 1 Maccabees says the Hasmoneans take the port of Joppa.

vignette.alt: A sandy harbour with small ships, a coastal town of pale houses, the sea opening west
vignette.caption: The port of Joppa (impression)

steps.text: In time, a Roman general will stand in Jerusalem, and this Hasmonean house will lose its independence. That is where our next chapter begins.
claims: In 63 BC a Roman general will take Jerusalem, and Hasmonean independence will end. That story belongs to the next chapter.

vignette.alt: Jerusalem on its hills under a long quiet sky, a road leading west, the story unfinished
vignette.caption: The story is not finished (impression)

steps.text: The story so far.
In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
claims: In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
steps.display: In 1207 BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.

steps.text: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.
claims: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.

steps.text: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.
claims: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.

steps.text: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.
claims: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.

steps.text: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.
claims: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.

steps.text: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about nine thirty BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
claims: How large their kingdom was is debated.
By about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
steps.display: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.

steps.text: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.
claims: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.

steps.text: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.
claims: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.

steps.text: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich, and the prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.
claims: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich.
The prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.

steps.text: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
claims: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
steps.display: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser III takes Damascus and Galilee, and in 722 BC Samaria falls.

steps.text: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.
claims: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.

steps.text: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.
claims: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.

steps.text: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings. Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.
claims: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings.
Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.

steps.text: Sennacherib is later killed by his own son. The city has been spared.
claims: Sennacherib is later killed by his own son. The city has been spared.

steps.text: Then Babylon takes Jerusalem and burns the city. Many are taken east; a remnant remains in the land of Benjamin.
claims: Babylon takes Jerusalem and burns the city.
Many are taken east; a remnant remains in Benjamin.

steps.text: Clay tablets in Babylon name Yaukin, king of Judah, still fed at the emperor's table. The Bible says the Temple was destroyed.
claims: Tablets in Babylon name Yaukin, king of Judah.
The Bible says the Temple was destroyed.

steps.text: The land is not empty, and a generation later a Persian king will take Babylon itself.
claims: The land is not empty, and a generation later a Persian king will take Babylon itself.

steps.text: Then a Persian king takes Babylon, without a battle in the Babylonian chronicle, and some of Judah's people come home.
claims: A Persian king takes Babylon without a battle, in the Babylonian chronicle.
Some of Judah's people come home.

steps.text: The land becomes Yehud, a small Persian province, not a restored kingdom of David. A temple stands again in Jerusalem.
claims: Yehud is a small Persian province, not a restored kingdom of David.
A temple stands again in Jerusalem, in the biblical account of a Second Temple.

steps.text: Jewish life now exists in two places: in Yehud, and among families who stay in the east. In time, new empires will come to this land.
claims: Jewish life continues both in Yehud and among families who stay in the east.
